title: ICMP Router Discovery Messages
summary: Specifies an extension of ICMP that lets hosts on multicast or broadcast networks discover the IP addresses of neighboring routers. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: ICMP Router Discovery lets a host learn the addresses of routers on its local link. Routers advertise periodically, and a host can ask for an advertisement when it starts.

questions: what is an icmp router advertisement
subtitle: Hosts learn neighboring router addresses from ICMP messages.

tldr.problem: A host needs a neighboring router address to send datagrams beyond its subnet, while manual lists cannot follow routers that become available or fail.
tldr.mechanism: Routers periodically send ICMP Router Advertisements; a host can send a Router Solicitation to request advertisements sooner.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can learn default routers without a routing protocol or a manually maintained list. The advertisements do not identify the best router for every destination.

today: RFC 1256 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1991. The work-unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Discovering a First-Hop Router
sections.content:
Before sending IP datagrams beyond its local subnet, a host needs the address of an operational router on that subnet. RFC 1256 defines an alternative to manually configured addresses or listening to routing protocols: two ICMP messages used on multicast links.

Router Advertisements announce neighboring router addresses. Router Solicitations let a host ask for advertisements sooner than the next periodic message. This mechanism finds neighboring routers but is not itself a routing protocol and does not choose the best router for each destination.
sections.plainLanguage: A host needs a local router before it can send traffic beyond its subnet. Routers announce their addresses, and hosts can ask them to announce sooner.

sections.title: Advertisement and Solicitation Messages
sections.content:
A Router Advertisement is ICMP type 9, code 0. It carries the number of router addresses, the entry size, a lifetime, and an address and preference level for each router.

A Router Solicitation is ICMP type 10, code 0, followed by a reserved field sent as zero. The lifetime tells hosts how long advertised addresses remain valid without another advertisement. Higher preference values are preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: An advertisement lists router addresses, their relative preference, and how long they remain valid. A solicitation asks routers on the link to send advertisements.

sections.title: Router Behavior
sections.content:
Each advertising router periodically sends advertisements on its multicast interfaces. It chooses a random interval between its configured minimum and maximum to reduce simultaneous messages from different routers.

For its first advertisements, the router caps the interval at 16 seconds. It also replies to valid solicitations, after a random delay of no more than 2 seconds. The default maximum interval is 600 seconds, and the default lifetime is three times that maximum.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers advertise at randomized intervals so they do not all send at once. After becoming available, a router sends its first few advertisements more often.

sections.title: Host Behavior
sections.content:
A host records neighboring router addresses learned from valid advertisements and sets a timer for each address using the advertised lifetime. A later advertisement updates the timer and preference; when the timer expires, the learned entry is removed.

After startup or certain interface changes, a host may send up to 3 solicitations. It stops soliciting after receiving a valid advertisement with a usable neighboring router address. A host never sends Router Advertisements.
sections.plainLanguage: A host keeps the routers it hears from and forgets an advertised router when its lifetime expires. Once it receives a usable answer, it stops asking for advertisements.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any system attached to a link can pretend to be a default router. Traffic sent through an impostor could be observed, dropped, or modified.

The RFC notes that these risks already exist on many broadcast links, and host configuration can disable dynamic discovery where the risk is unacceptable. Authentication for advertisements is identified as further study, not specified by this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A malicious system on the same link could advertise itself as a router and affect traffic. Hosts can disable discovery when that risk is unacceptable.
